title: Two forms of the Latin rite
word: Two forms of the Latin rite
hookLine: the Mass of 1970 and the older Latin Mass both have devoted followers, with strong feelings

lines: ENGLISH AND SINGING. LATIN AND CHANT.
BOTH LOVE WHAT THEY WENT TO.
cards: Two friends meet for brunch after Sunday Mass. They went to different churches.
One went to a Mass in English: the priest facing the people across the altar, the whole room singing the responses, his opening words in her own language.
The other went to a Latin Mass: chant, long silences, the priest facing the same way as the people, toward the altar, beginning at its foot with a psalm in Latin. Both love what they went to.
Both have, at some point, said something sharp about the other's. Neither of them is leaving the Church.

teach.h: THE REFORMED MISSAL AFTER THE COUNCIL.
teach.b: After the Second Vatican Council, Pope Paul VI issued a revised Roman Missal: the Mass in the reformed books, usually in the local language.

teach.h: THE OLDER MASS: TO THE ALTAR OF GOD.
teach.b: The older Missal, used before the reform, gives the Latin Mass. It opens with prayers at the foot of the altar, built on a psalm. In the Douay-Rheims: "I will go in to the altar of God: to God who giveth joy to my youth."
Some drawn to the older Mass speak of reverence, silence, and continuity with the generations who prayed it.
Some drawn to the reformed Mass speak of hearing the readings in their own tongue, a wider sweep of scripture, and joining aloud in the prayers.
The popes have handled this differently. Pope Benedict XVI widened permission for the older Mass and described the two as two expressions of the one Roman rite.
Pope Francis later placed the older Mass under each bishop's oversight and taught that the reformed books are the one expression of the Roman rite's law of prayer.

Some Catholics on each side have felt each decision deeply. Here is what both Masses share: the same sacrifice of Christ, made present; the same Gospels proclaimed; the same Lord received in communion.
And one prayer prayed in both: the old Roman Canon, kept in the reformed Missal as the first Eucharistic Prayer.

teach.h: THAT THERE BE NO SCHISMS AMONG YOU.
teach.b: Paul begged a divided church in Corinth, in the Douay-Rheims, "that there be no schisms among you." Strong feelings, held by people who are in one Church.

how: Latin Catholic parishes celebrate the Mass in the reformed Roman Missal, usually in the local language; some communities, with their bishop's permission, celebrate the older Latin Mass. Catholics may attend either, and both are celebrated as the one sacrifice of the Mass.

games.q: you're at a Mass in the reformed Missal, and the priest begins the first Eucharistic Prayer. a friend who loves the Latin Mass is beside you. what's she hearing?
o: a prayer written new for the reformed Mass.
the old Roman Canon, the same prayer at the heart of her Latin Mass.
a prayer borrowed from the Eastern churches.
games.why: the first Eucharistic Prayer is the Roman Canon, kept in the reformed Missal. the two Masses share it.

practice: Bring to mind one real person who loves a form of the Mass you don't, in the pew at the moment they care about most.
If you pray, ask God for peace between Catholics who love different forms of the Mass, and name that person; if you don't, hold them with good will, and let one sharp sentence go.

wordCard.voice: Two forms of the Latin rite. The reformed Mass from after the Second Vatican Council and the older Latin Mass: both Roman, both offering the one sacrifice, both deeply loved. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin, the law of praying is the law of believing: an old saying that ties how the Church prays to what it believes.

carryVoice: Your line: one church, both loved. The same Lord is received at both altars. That's today, done.
